rows.gloss: by being of the nature of reflective awareness
through union with emission and projection
rows.grounds: by the joining of outpouring and casting forth

items.question: How is the God of gods, Bhairava, characterized in this state?
premises: The God of gods is Bhairava, possessed of full power.
Bhairava is of the nature of reflective awareness.
Bhairava is connected with the union of emission and projection.
items.inference: Bhairava is the fully empowered supreme reality whose reflective awareness expresses itself through emission and projection.
uncertainties: The exact technical nuance of visarga and ākṣepa in this context may vary by commentary.
items.plain_english: To this extent, the God of gods, Bhairava, possessed of full power, is of the nature of reflective awareness and is united with emission and projection.

rows.grounds: because of cognition that determines a fixed extent

items.question: Why are these powers called Kalikas and how is the supreme described in the Sara scripture?
premises: These powers are called Kalikas because of knowledge that measures limitation.
This naming is found in some sources.
The revered Sara scripture also speaks of a supreme one-syllabled power in the middle.
items.inference: The Kalikas are named from limiting cognition, while the Sara scripture points to a supreme single-syllabled power at the center.
uncertainties: The identity of the one syllable is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: Because of knowledge that measures limitation, these powers are called Kalikas in some places; and in the revered Sara scripture, the supreme one-syllabled power is said to be in the middle.

rows.gloss: one should worship the one called Bhairava-self
rows.grounds: worship her named as the self of Bhairava
encircled by a group of twelve yoginis

items.question: How should the Bhairava-self power be worshipped and how far does her circle extend?
premises: The power called Bhairava-self should be worshipped.
She is surrounded by twelve yoginis.
From those powers the circle extends up to sixty-four.
items.inference: Worship of the Bhairava-self centers on a twelvefold circle that unfolds into a larger circle of sixty-four powers.
uncertainties: The ritual details of the worship are not given in this verse.
items.plain_english: One should worship the power called the Bhairava-self, surrounded by twelve yoginis; from them the circle of powers extends up to sixty-four.

rows.gloss: in many ways in the scripture

items.question: How far does the unfolding of these powers go and how are they named?
premises: The unfolding proceeds from the syllable e up to the thousand-spoked.
The powers have different functions.
Their names are given in many ways in the scripture.
items.inference: The power-circle expands vastly from a phonemic starting point, and its members receive varied names according to function and scriptural teaching.
uncertainties: The phrase sahasrāra may be symbolic or technical depending on context.
items.plain_english: Beginning from the syllable e, it unfolds up to the thousand-spoked; and in the scripture these powers are given many names according to their different functions.

rows.gloss: through forms of duality, nonduality, and mixture
rows.grounds: by the joining of dual, nondual, and mixed modes

items.question: Where are the modes of worship of these powers explained in detail?
premises: The worships take dual, nondual, and mixed forms.
The revered Traishira discusses this subject.
It explains the matter at great length.
items.inference: The Traishira scripture gives an extensive account of worship in dual, nondual, and mixed modes.
uncertainties: The exact scope of the Traishira's discussion is not summarized here.
items.plain_english: Their modes of worship, in dual, nondual, and mixed forms, have been explained at great length in the revered Traishira.

rows.gloss: from fear of prolixity and from lack of usefulness
rows.grounds: because of fear of expansion and because it is not useful here

items.question: Why is the detailed account not written here, and how are these powers described?
premises: The detailed account is not written here.
It is omitted for fear of prolixity and because it is not useful in this context.
The same powers are proclaimed as stainless, pure, and not-terrible.
items.inference: The author omits extensive ritual detail here while affirming the essential purity and benign nature of these powers.
items.plain_english: It is not written here, for fear of prolixity and because it is not needed; those same powers are proclaimed as stainless, pure, and not-terrible.

rows.gloss: of the terrible and more terrible
and because of being the source
rows.grounds: and because they give rise to them

rows.gloss: in the transcendence of those three limiting conditions
rows.grounds: beyond the triad of those conditions

items.question: How can the pure powers also be related to terrible forms and cosmic functions?
premises: The powers are the source of the terrible and more terrible forms.
Because they are their source, they are of that nature as well.
Their forms operate in creation, maintenance, dissolution, and beyond those three conditions.
items.inference: The same powers appear as benign in essence yet also manifest as fierce forms and as the basis of the three cosmic acts and their transcendence.
uncertainties: The verse compresses several doctrinal relations into a short statement.
items.plain_english: Because they are the source of the terrible and more terrible forms, they are also of that nature, appearing in creation, maintenance, dissolution, and in the transcendence of those three conditions.

items.question: How do the teachers classify the form of these powers beyond limiting conditions?
premises: The abiding form of these powers is divided in many ways.
There is a form beyond limiting conditions.
The teachers declare that transcendent form to be twofold.
items.inference: Although the powers appear in many divisions, their condition-transcending form is taught as twofold.
items.plain_english: The abiding form of those same powers is divided in many ways, but the teachers say that the form beyond limiting conditions is twofold.

rows.gloss: from the non-arising of limiting conditions
by the method of forceful ripening
rows.grounds: through the process of intense maturation

items.question: What are the two ways the transcendent state can be understood?
premises: The transcendent state may be due to the non-arising of limiting conditions.
It may also be due to the calming of limiting conditions.
That calming is twofold: by quieting and by forceful ripening.
items.inference: The condition-transcending state is reached either because conditions do not arise or because they are pacified, and pacification itself occurs in two distinct ways.
uncertainties: The practical difference between śānti and haṭhapāka is only indicated, not fully explained.
items.plain_english: This may be because limiting conditions do not arise, or because they are calmed; and that calming is twofold, either by quieting or by the method of forceful ripening.

rows.gloss: by what is called the savor of devouring
rows.grounds: through the relish known as assimilation

items.question: Which form of pacification is especially suited for instruction, and what does it accomplish?
premises: Pacification by forceful ripening works through the continual blazing savor of devouring.
This is presented as the third form in the discussion.
It burns up the fuel of difference.
items.inference: The forceful-ripening pacification is especially suitable for instruction because it actively consumes the sense of difference.
uncertainties: The numbering as 'third' depends on the immediately preceding classification.
items.plain_english: The pacification called forceful ripening, fully active through the continual blazing savor of devouring, is the one fit for instruction, because it burns up the fuel of difference.

rows.gloss: in the fire in the belly of one's own awareness
rows.grounds: in the digestive fire of innate knowing

items.question: What happens when all things are forcefully offered into the fire of one's own awareness?
premises: All things are forcefully offered into the fire of one's own awareness.
By their own power they kindle that fire.
As a result they abandon the division of difference.
items.inference: When all phenomena are offered into innate awareness, they fuel that awareness and lose their apparent separateness.
items.plain_english: When all things are forcefully offered into the fire of one's own awareness, they kindle that fire by their own power and abandon the division of difference.

rows.gloss: they consume what has become nectar
rows.grounds: they eat the world transformed into immortality

items.question: What do the goddesses of consciousness do when the divided forms of things are dissolved?
premises: Forceful ripening dissolves the divided forms of things.
The universe becomes transformed into nectar.
The goddesses of consciousness consume that nectar-like universe.
items.inference: When separateness is dissolved, consciousness-powers assimilate the whole universe as nectar.
items.plain_english: When, by forceful ripening, the divided forms of things are dissolved, the goddesses of consciousness consume the whole universe as it becomes nectar.

rows.gloss: resting solely in the full heart
rows.grounds: lying exclusively in the plenary heart

rows.gloss: Bhairava of the sky of consciousness
rows.grounds: Bhairava who is the space of awareness

rows.gloss: they repose upon the god without difference
rows.grounds: they rest in nonseparation upon that deity

items.question: What do the satisfied goddesses of consciousness do after consuming the universe as nectar?
premises: The goddesses of consciousness become satisfied.
Bhairava rests solely in the full heart of their own self as the sky of consciousness.
They repose upon that Bhairava without difference.
items.inference: After assimilation, the powers of consciousness come to rest in nondual union with Bhairava, the space of awareness.
items.plain_english: Satisfied, they repose without difference upon the god Bhairava, the sky of consciousness, who rests solely in the full heart of their own self.

rows.gloss: from entry into acts and functions and from the multiplicity of names and worships
rows.grounds: because of immersion in activities and because names and worships are many

rows.gloss: the form appears even in non-difference
rows.grounds: the form shines forth even though there is no difference

items.question: How can these powers appear in many forms while remaining non-different?
premises: The powers enter into various acts and functions.
They are associated with many names and modes of worship.
Even so, their manifold form appears within non-difference.
items.inference: Multiplicity of function, name, and worship does not contradict the underlying non-difference of these powers.
items.plain_english: Thus, because of their entry into various acts and functions and because of the many names and forms of worship, their manifold form appears even within non-difference.

rows.gloss: of the goddesses through the joining of invocation and dismissal
rows.grounds: of the goddesses by the practice of bringing in and sending out

rows.gloss: by one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine and more
rows.grounds: through increasing numbers beginning with one and going beyond nine

items.question: How is the expansion of these goddesses described in terms of number?
premises: The same goddesses are considered.
Their manifestation involves invocation and dismissal.
Their expansion is described through increasing numerical groupings.
items.inference: The goddess-powers unfold in ordered numerical expansions through ritual processes of invocation and dismissal.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically compressed and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: And of these very goddesses, through the joining of invocation and dismissal, there is an expansion by groups of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and more.

rows.gloss: the extensive division beginning with Rudra, Arka, Anya, Kala, Sena, and so on
rows.grounds: the broad differentiation starting from Rudra, Arka, Anya, Kala, Sena, etc.

rows.gloss: now to the matter at hand

items.question: Why does the text turn away from further enumeration at this point?
premises: The divisions of the powers extend widely, beginning with Rudra, Arka, Anya, Kala, Sena, and others.
Further elaboration would be excessive.
The discussion now turns to the matter at hand.
items.inference: The author acknowledges the vastness of the enumerations but deliberately returns to the main topic.
uncertainties: The exact referents of the listed names depend on tantric doctrinal context.
items.plain_english: The extensive division beginning with Rudra, Arka, Anya, Kala, Sena, and so on is vast; enough of further detail—now the discussion turns to the matter at hand.

rows.grounds: in the manner of a reflected image

items.question: How does the entire multiplicity of things appear in consciousness, and who realizes this?
premises: The whole expanded group of things appears in the self of consciousness.
It appears as a reflection.
One for whom it appears thus is the Lord of the universe.
items.inference: To see all multiplicity as a reflection in consciousness is to stand in the realization of universal lordship.
items.plain_english: This whole expanded group of things shines in the self of consciousness as a reflection; one for whom it appears thus is indeed the Lord of the universe.

rows.gloss: for whom such a non-conceptual awareness
rows.grounds: who has this kind of thought-free recognition
sealed by the method of Shambhu

items.question: What characterizes a person who is established in the Shambhava means?
premises: Such a person has a non-conceptual reflective awareness in the self.
That awareness is ever arising.
This state is marked by the Shambhava means.
items.inference: Constant non-conceptual self-recognition is the sign of one established in the Shambhava means.
items.plain_english: One in whom such a non-conceptual reflective awareness is ever arising in the self is indeed marked by the Shambhava means.

rows.gloss: the reflective awareness of full I-ness
mantra, mudra, ritual action, and worship other than that
rows.grounds: other practices such as mantra, gesture, rite, and worship

items.question: What practices are required in this Shambhava realization beyond full I-consciousness?
premises: The realization explained here is the reflective awareness of full I-ness.
Other practices include mantra, mudra, ritual action, and worship.
None of those other practices are required here.
items.inference: In this mode, direct recognition of full I-consciousness stands apart from auxiliary ritual techniques.
items.plain_english: This is the reflective awareness of full I-ness that has been explained; here there are no other practices such as mantra, mudra, ritual action, or worship.

rows.grounds: known by the further name of living liberation

items.question: What result comes from repeatedly resorting to this non-conceptual immersion?
premises: One repeatedly resorts to this non-conceptual immersion.
That immersion leads to the state of Bhairava.
That state is also called liberation while living.
items.inference: Repeated non-conceptual immersion culminates in Bhairava-hood, which is living liberation.
items.plain_english: Resorting again and again to this non-conceptual immersion, one attains the state of Bhairava, also called liberation while living.

rows.gloss: even by a brief indication there is this framing of means and goal
rows.grounds: even in summary form the distinction of method and object is set out

items.question: What new topic begins to be examined from this point onward?
premises: From this point onward, liberation while living is examined.
In this examination, the framing of means and goal is indicated even briefly.
This marks a shift in the discussion.
items.inference: The text now turns to a systematic consideration of living liberation, including the relation of means and goal.
items.plain_english: From this point onward, liberation while living is examined, where even in brief outline the distinction between means and goal is set forth.

rows.grounds: thus in the path without means

items.question: Why could liberation not be discussed in terms of means and goal in the previous chapter?
premises: In the previous chapter there was not even a notion of difference.
That chapter concerned the means-less path.
Where there is no difference, questions of who is liberated, how, and from what do not properly arise.
items.inference: The previous chapter's nondual, means-less standpoint excluded the framework of means, goal, and liberation as distinct terms.
items.plain_english: But in the previous chapter there was not even a notion of difference; therefore, in that means-less path, who is liberated, how, or from what?

items.question: How should the wise person relate the earlier fiftyfold scheme to the Shambhava means?
premises: The Shambhava means is a non-conceptual reflective awareness.
A fiftyfold division was previously indicated.
The wise person should apply that earlier scheme here.
items.inference: The earlier fiftyfold framework is to be understood within the non-conceptual recognition of the Shambhava means.
uncertainties: The verse assumes familiarity with the previously indicated fiftyfold division.
items.plain_english: In the non-conceptual reflective awareness called the Shambhava means, the wise person should apply the fiftyfold division that was indicated earlier.

rows.grounds: even the element earth, in a thought-free way
beholding, reaches the state of Bhairava

rows.gloss: this same method applies also to water and the rest
rows.grounds: this procedure holds for water and so on as well

items.question: How can even the element earth become a support for realizing Bhairava-hood?
premises: Even the earth can be seen without conceptualization.
It can be seen as reflected in one's own self.
The same method applies to water and the other elements.
items.inference: Non-conceptual recognition of any element as a reflection in the self leads to Bhairava-hood.
items.plain_english: Seeing even the earth itself, without conceptualization, as reflected in one's own self, one attains Bhairava-hood; the same method applies to water and the other elements as well.
